learningObjective: Understand tl.constexpr as a compile-time specialization mechanism vs runtime scalars.

canonicalClaims.claim: `tl.constexpr` marks a kernel argument as compile-time; each distinct value triggers a fresh specialized compile, enabling loop unrolling, vector sizing, and constant folding. Non-constexpr scalars are runtime values shared by all invocations.
nonImplications: Does not imply constexpr is always beneficial.
Does not imply pointer arguments are constexpr by default.

misconceptions.claim: `tl.constexpr` is only an IDE type hint.
misconceptions.whyWrong: It has semantic effect on the JIT.

misconceptions.claim: Every distinct value of any scalar argument re-compiles the kernel.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Only constexpr changes force re-compile; non-constexpr scalars reuse.

misconceptions.claim: Promoting shape dims like `N` to constexpr is always faster.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Compile-time blow-up and cache pressure may outweigh gains.

implementationFacts: Triton also specializes on pointer alignment (16-byte) and value divisibility (`divisible_by`) attributes.
TRITON_CACHE_DIR caches compiled kernels across processes.
